name: All Beer
description: Every recognized beer style, nested and grouped by similarity.

children.name: Ales
children.description: Top-fermented British, Irish, American and related ales (excluding Belgian, wheat, sour and hybrid styles): bitters, browns, pale ales, IPAs, porters, stouts and strong ales.

children.name: British Bitters & Pale Ales
children.description: Amber-to-gold English session ales built on pale ale malt, English hops and fruity British yeast; traditionally served on cask.

children.name: Ordinary Bitter
children.description: Low-gravity, easy-drinking cask bitter with moderate bitterness, bready/biscuity malt, light caramel and earthy-floral English hops.
malts: Touch of amber or dark malt for colour
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

parents.note: BJCP: the family of British bitters grew out of English pale ales as a draught product after the late 1800s.

children.name: Best Bitter
children.description: A step up in strength from ordinary bitter: balanced bitterness, toasty/caramel malt and English hop character, with fruity esters.
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

parents.note: Grew out of draught pale ale alongside ordinary bitter; traditionally the brewer's premium draught bitter.

children.name: Strong Bitter (ESB)
children.description: Stronger, fuller bitter (includes ESB) with richer caramel/toffee malt, firm bitterness and pronounced English hop and ester character.
malts: Touch of black malt for colour
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

parents.note: BJCP: strong bitters can be seen as a higher-gravity version of best bitters.
BJCP: bottled British pale ale roughly approximates a strong bitter (though historically the styles differed).

children.name: English Pale Ale
children.description: Bottled/keg cousin of the bitters: golden-to-copper, biscuity malt, moderate earthy-herbal English hops; not a separate BJCP style (judged as bitter), defined by BA as Classic English-Style Pale Ale.
children.yeast: English ale yeast; Burton strains for sulfate-driven dryness
children.yearLabel: c.1700 (term 'pale ale' first recorded 1703); Burton pale ales 1820s–40s

children.name: British Golden Ale
children.description: Pale, refreshing hop-forward session ale created as a summer alternative to lager; clean malt canvas with citrusy or floral hops.
malts: Low-colour pale ale malt or lager malt

parents.note: Very pale, hop-forward 'golden bitters' created to win back lager drinkers; also called Golden Bitters.

children.name: Australian Sparkling Ale
children.description: Bottle-conditioned, highly carbonated pale ale with fruity esters, bready malt and earthy-herbal Australian hops (Pride of Ringwood).
malts: Small amount of crystal for colour
children.yeast: Coopers-type Australian ale yeast, bottle conditioned

topSellers.name: Coopers Extra Strong Vintage Ale (stronger 7.5% variant, above style range)

parents.note: Bottled Australian ale was developed to compete with imported bottled British pale ales such as Bass.

children.name: Scottish & Irish Ales
children.description: Malt-forward, lightly hopped ales from Scotland and Ireland: clean, caramel-to-toasty, with dry roasty finishes in the Irish red.

children.name: Scottish Light (60/-)
children.description: Very low-strength, malt-focused dark amber ale with light caramel, toast and a dry, slightly roasty finish; minimal hops.
malts: Small amount of roasted barley or black malt
children.yearLabel: post-WWII modern form (shilling names used earlier for mild ales)

parents.note: Post-WWII Scottish 60/-, 70/- and 80/- were the Scottish breweries' three draught pale ales (Light, Heavy, Export), parti-gyled together; unrelated to 19th-century shilling ales of the same names.
Pattinson: some 60/- was brewed to the same recipe as the stronger pale ales but coloured darker to resemble Dark Mild; Usher's brewed both a 60/- Mild and a 60/- Pale Ale.

children.name: Scottish Heavy (70/-)
children.description: Session-strength amber Scottish ale: caramel, toasted malt and a dry finish, with very low hop character.
malts: Small amount of roasted barley or black malt
children.yearLabel: post-WWII modern form (shilling names used earlier for mild ales)

parents.note: Post-WWII Scottish 60/-, 70/- and 80/- were the Scottish breweries' three draught pale ales (Light, Heavy, Export), parti-gyled together; unrelated to 19th-century shilling ales of the same names.

children.name: Scottish Export (80/-)
children.description: The strongest of the session Scottish ales: richer caramel, toffee and toasted malt with a clean, dry finish.
malts: Small amount of roasted barley or black malt
children.yearLabel: post-WWII modern form (shilling names used earlier for mild ales)

parents.note: Post-WWII Scottish 60/-, 70/- and 80/- were the Scottish breweries' three draught pale ales (Light, Heavy, Export), parti-gyled together; unrelated to 19th-century shilling ales of the same names.

children.name: Irish Red Ale
children.description: Easy-drinking, clean red-amber ale with caramel/toffee sweetness up front and a dry, lightly roasted finish.

origin.era: 20th century (modern style adapted from English bitter); revived as a craft style

malts: Roasted barley (for colour and dry finish)

parents.note: BJCP: essentially an adaptation of the popular English bitter with less hopping and a little roast; Cornell calls the 'Irish red' tradition largely a marketing construct.

children.name: Brown & Amber Ales
children.description: Caramel, nutty, toffee and chocolate-tinged ales from mild and brown ale traditions in Britain and their hoppier American descendants.

children.name: Dark Mild
children.description: Low-gravity, malt-driven dark ale with chocolate, caramel and light roast; soft body and very restrained hops.
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)
children.yearLabel: 1800s X ales; dark brown only after WWI

children.name: British Brown Ale
children.description: Malty, caramel-nutty brown ale with toffee and light chocolate notes and moderate English hop bitterness.
malts: British mild or pale ale malt
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

children.name: London Brown Ale
children.description: Historical, very sweet, low-alcohol dark brown ale with caramel, toffee and dried-fruit flavours and minimal bitterness; often sweetened after fermentation.
malts: High proportion of dark crystal malt

topSellers.name: Forest Brown (historical; discontinued, no current third example)

children.name: American Brown Ale
children.description: Malty, chocolate-caramel brown ale with more bitterness and citrusy/piney American hop character than its British parent.

parents.note: Pete Slosberg built Pete's Wicked Ale (1986) trying to copy Samuel Smith's Nut Brown Ale; later hopped up American-style.

children.name: American Amber / Red Ale
children.description: Amber-to-red ale balancing caramel malt sweetness with citrusy, piney American hops; includes most American 'red ales'.

parents.note: BJCP: developed as a variation from American Pale Ales.
Early US micros brewed amber-coloured ESBs; Full Sail's James Emmerson called English ESB the source material for American amber.

children.name: American Pale & Blonde Ales
children.description: Pale, clean American ales: hop-led pale ales and soft, approachable blonde ales.

children.name: American Pale Ale
children.description: Pale, refreshing, hop-forward ale with citrus/pine American hops over a clean, lightly bready malt base; the beer that launched US craft.

parents.note: BJCP: a modern American craft-era adaptation of English pale ale using indigenous ingredients.

children.name: Blonde Ale
children.description: Easy-drinking, pale golden craft ale with soft bready malt, light fruity or floral hops and a clean finish; a craft 'gateway' beer.
children.yeast: Clean American ale yeast, Kölsch or lager yeast

children.name: IPAs
children.description: India Pale Ales and their many modern variants: hop-forward, bitter-to-juicy pale ales.

children.name: IPA (India Pale Ale)
children.description: Hop-forward pale ale family, from earthy English originals to resinous West Coast, juicy hazy and strong double versions; IPA is roughly half of US craft off-premise dollar sales. Ranges shown span the BJCP-defined IPA styles (12C, 21A-C, 22A); session and triple IPAs fall outside them.
children.yeast: Clean American or attenuative English ale yeast

children.name: English IPA
children.description: Hoppy, moderately strong pale ale with earthy, floral and marmalade English hops, biscuity malt and a dry finish.

parents.note: BJCP: the East India Company had Allsopp recreate and reformulate the London pale stock ale in Burton in 1823; White Shield traces to 1829.

children.name: American IPA
children.description: Decidedly hoppy and bitter pale ale with citrus, pine, resin and tropical American hops over a clean, dry malt base.

parents.note: BJCP: the first modern American craft adaptation of the traditional English style, using whole Cascade hops.

children.name: West Coast IPA
children.description: Bone-dry, crystal-clear, very bitter IPA showcasing piney, resinous and citrus hops over a minimal pale malt base; BA-recognised separately since 2023 (BJCP judges it as American IPA).
children.yeast: Clean, highly attenuative American ale yeast (Chico)

parents.note: BJCP: dry, sharply bitter, clear examples known as West Coast IPA are really just a type of American IPA; refined in 1990s Southern California.

children.name: Hazy IPA (New England IPA)
children.description: Opaque, soft and juicy IPA with intense tropical/stone-fruit hop aroma, low perceived bitterness and a creamy, full mouthfeel.
children.yeast: Estery English or American ale yeast (e.g. London Ale III), with biotransformation dry hopping

parents.note: BJCP: originated in New England as an American IPA variant; Heady Topper the original inspiration.

children.name: Double IPA (Imperial IPA)
children.description: Intensely hoppy, strong, dry IPA with big citrus/pine/tropical hop flavour, high bitterness and a clean, sugar-lightened body.

origin.era: Mid-late 1990s (Vinnie Cilurzo's Inaugural Ale at Blind Pig, 1994; popularised by Pliny the Elder, 2000)

children.yearLabel: 1994 (Blind Pig Inaugural Ale); Pliny the Elder 2000

parents.note: BJCP: an American craft innovation of the mid-late 1990s as a more intense version of American IPA.

children.name: Triple IPA
children.description: An informal super-strong extension of the double IPA, roughly 10% ABV and up, with enormous hop saturation and a still-dry finish; not recognised by BJCP or BA.

parents.note: Pliny the Younger was conceived as an amped-up version of the double IPA Pliny the Elder.

children.name: Session IPA
children.description: Lower-alcohol IPA (5% ABV or less; most commercial examples 3.5-5%) that keeps a full IPA hop aroma and bitterness in a light, dry body; BJCP judges it as a session-strength 21B Specialty IPA, and BA sets the floor at 0.5% ABV.
malts: Light crystal or dextrin malt for body

parents.note: BJCP: a Session IPA is a Specialty IPA with American IPA as its base style at session strength.

children.name: Black IPA (Cascadian Dark Ale)
children.description: Black-coloured IPA: American IPA hop intensity with light, dry roast from debittered dark malt and little burnt character.

origin.era: c. 1990 (Greg Noonan's Blackwatch IPA, Vermont Pub & Brewery); popular early 2010s

children.yearLabel: c.1990 (Greg Noonan's Blackwatch IPA); fad early 2010s

parents.note: BJCP: an American IPA variant first commercially produced by Greg Noonan around 1990.

children.name: White IPA
children.description: Fruity, spicy, refreshing cross of a Belgian witbier and an American IPA: wheat body, Belgian yeast spice and citrusy hops.

parents.note: BJCP: a craft interpretation of American IPA crossed with a Witbier.
Developed as a spring seasonal to appeal to Witbier and IPA drinkers alike.

children.name: Red IPA
children.description: Hoppy, bitter, strong amber-red IPA where caramel and toffee malt support citrusy/piney American hops.

parents.note: BJCP: based on American IPA but with the malt flavours of an American Amber Ale.
BJCP: Red Tail-style amber ales were the progenitor of Red IPAs.

children.name: Rye IPA
children.description: American IPA with a generous portion of rye malt adding a dry, spicy, grainy edge to the hop character.

topSellers.name: Ruthless Rye IPA (historical; retired 2015, occasional small-batch revivals)

parents.note: BJCP: a modern craft-era variation of American IPA, popular among homebrewers.

children.name: Brown IPA
children.description: Hoppy, bitter brown ale: chocolate and caramel malt flavours with American IPA hop intensity and dryness.
children.yearLabel: 1980s–90s homebrew 'Texas brown'; Dogfish Head Indian Brown 1999

parents.note: BJCP: the hoppier, stronger homebrew-era American browns are now classed as Brown IPA.
Brewed to IPA strength and hopping (Dogfish Head calls Indian Brown the prototypical dark IPA).

children.name: Belgian IPA
children.description: IPA fermented with Belgian Tripel/golden strong ale yeast: fruity-spicy phenolic yeast character, high carbonation and assertive hops.

parents.note: BJCP: homebrewers and craft brewers substituted Belgian yeast in their American IPA recipes.
BJCP: Belgian breweries typically added more hops to their stronger pale beers (Houblon Chouffe is billed 'Dobbelen IPA Tripel').

children.name: Brut IPA
children.description: Very pale, bone-dry, highly carbonated IPA fermented with amyloglucosidase enzyme; champagne-like, aromatic and low in bitterness. A 2018-19 fad that has largely disappeared from production.
malts: Pilsner or very pale base malt
children.yeast: Neutral ale yeast plus amyloglucosidase enzyme
adjuncts: Rice, corn or other adjuncts (up to 40%)

parents.note: BJCP: a west-coast reaction to hazy and milkshake IPAs, made bone-dry with enzymes.

children.name: Cold IPA
children.description: 'Wester than West Coast' IPA: crisp, clear and dry, fermented warm with lager yeast and brewed with rice or corn, then heavily dry-hopped; not yet a BJCP or BA style.

parents.note: Kevin Davey's West Coast-style IPA brewed lager-style for a crisp, dry finish.
Uses the American adjunct-lager toolkit: 20–40% rice or corn in the grist and lager yeast (fermented warm).

children.yearLabel: late 1700s (Hodgson's pale ale to India by 1793; name 'IPA' c.1830s)

parents.note: A pale, well-hopped stock (October-type) ale shipped to India; Hodgson of Bow exported pale ale from at least 1793.

children.name: Porters & Stouts
children.description: Dark ales built on roasted, chocolate and brown malts, from London porter and dry Irish stout to sweet, tropical and imperial strengths.

children.name: English Porter
children.description: Moderate-strength brown-to-black London ale with chocolate, toffee and bready brown-malt flavours and gentle roast.
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

children.name: American Porter
children.description: Robust, roasty dark ale with chocolate and coffee malt, more bitterness and American hop character than English porter.
children.yeast: Clean American or characterful English ale yeast

parents.note: BJCP: a stronger, more aggressive version of earlier Pre-Prohibition Porters...
...or English Porters, first brewed in the modern craft beer era.

children.name: Baltic Porter
children.description: Strong, smooth dark beer with dark fruit, caramel, toffee and chocolate; usually lager-fermented (grouped here with porters by lineage, though BJCP places it in 9 Strong European Beer).

origin.country: Baltic region (Poland, Finland, Russia, Baltic states)

topSellers.name: Baltika No. 6 Porter
topSellers.brewery: Baltika (VG Invest since Dec 2024; formerly Carlsberg)

parents.note: BJCP: developed in Baltic countries after imports of popular English porters and stouts were interrupted in the early 1800s; later adapted to bottom fermentation.
The strong English export stouts (imperial stout) shipped to the Baltic were the other model.

children.name: Pre-Prohibition Porter
children.description: Historical American porter: lighter-bodied, low roast, often brewed with lager yeast and adjuncts such as corn, molasses or porterine.
malts: Low percentages of black, chocolate and brown malt
children.yearLabel: 19th century (porter brewed in Philadelphia from the 1770s; lager methods after 1850)

parents.note: BJCP: brewed in Philadelphia from the revolutionary period as an adaptation of English beer, later modified by German immigrant lager brewers.

children.name: Irish Stout
children.description: Black, dry, roasty stout with coffee-like roasted barley, firm bitterness and a creamy (often nitro) body; low alcohol.
children.yearLabel: c.1810 (Guinness 'stouter kind of porter'); diverged late 1800s

parents.note: BJCP: evolved from London porters; Guinness brewed only porter from 1799 and a stouter porter from around 1810.

children.name: Irish Extra Stout
children.description: Fuller, stronger bottled Irish stout with more roast, chocolate and coffee depth and a dry, bitter finish.

parents.note: BJCP: same roots as Irish Stout but a stronger, mainly bottled product.

children.name: Sweet / Milk Stout
children.description: Full-bodied, sweet, creamy stout with milk-chocolate and coffee flavours; residual sweetness usually from lactose.

parents.note: Porter was the predecessor of all stouts; sweet/milk stout was an English stout of the early 1900s sweetened with lactose.

children.name: Oatmeal Stout
children.description: Smooth, silky dark stout where oats add body and a nutty, grainy depth to coffee and chocolate roast.

parents.note: BJCP: a variant of nourishing/invalid stouts c.1900 using oats, developed independently of sweet stout; porter was the predecessor of all stouts.

children.name: Tropical Stout
children.description: Sweet, fruity, strong stout popular in the Caribbean and Asia: smooth roast, high esters and clean sugar-boosted strength.

parents.note: BJCP: a local adaptation of Foreign Extra Stouts brewed with indigenous ingredients in the Caribbean and other tropical markets.

children.name: Foreign Extra Stout
children.description: Strong, roasty, export-strength stout with coffee, chocolate and dark-fruit notes and firm bitterness; dominant in Africa and the Caribbean.

parents.note: BJCP: stronger, more heavily hopped export stouts (stout porters) of the 18th–19th centuries; Guinness' West India Porter of 1801 became Foreign Extra Stout.

children.name: American Stout
children.description: Roasty, bitter, full-flavoured stout with coffee and dark chocolate and often noticeable American hop character.

parents.note: BJCP: applied aggressive American hopping to a strong traditional English or Irish stout.

children.name: Imperial Stout
children.description: Intensely flavoured, big, dark ale with deep roast, dark fruit, chocolate and warming alcohol; ranges from British fruity-malty to American roasty-hoppy.
children.yeast: English or American ale yeast (alcohol tolerant)

children.name: American Imperial Stout
children.description: Big, roasty, intensely bitter imperial stout with more pronounced roast, hop bitterness and often American hop aroma than British versions.

parents.note: BJCP: embraced in the US craft era as an adaptation extending the style with American hops and roast.

children.name: British Imperial Stout
children.description: The original 'Russian' imperial stout: rich dark fruit, treacle and chocolate with balanced roast, fruity esters and moderate bitterness.

origin.era: Late 18th century (Thrale's/Barclay Perkins for the Russian court)

children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

parents.note: The English line: Barclay Perkins' Imperial Brown Stout, brewed continuously until 1993; revived in the craft era as an export.

children.yearLabel: 1780s (Thrale's strong export stout for the Russian court)

parents.note: BJCP: traces roots to strong English porters brewed for export in the 1700s; stouts were originally called 'stout porters'.

children.name: Pastry Stout
children.description: Strong, very sweet dessert-like stout flavoured to evoke pastries and confections (vanilla, chocolate, maple, coconut, fruit), often with lactose; judged under BA's 'Dessert or Pastry Beer' (2026; 'Dessert Stout or Pastry Stout' from 2023), whose colour range runs 13-40+ SRM, stouts being the dark end.

parents.note: Usually built on an imperial stout base loaded with dessert adjuncts (lactose, vanilla, cacao, etc.).

children.name: Strong Ales
children.description: High-gravity British and American ales: malty, warming and often aged, from old ales and wee heavies to barleywines and wheatwines.

children.name: British Strong Ale
children.description: Malty, fruity, warming ale above bitter strength, with caramel, toffee and dried-fruit flavours; broad catch-all for strong British ales.
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

children.name: Old Ale
children.description: Strong, malty ale showing aged character: dark fruit, toffee, sherry-like oxidation and sometimes light tartness or Brett.
children.yeast: Characterful British ale yeast (e.g. London/Fuller's, Whitbread or Yorkshire strains)

children.name: Wee Heavy (Strong Scotch Ale)
children.description: Rich, malty, caramel-forward strong Scottish ale with toffee, plum and a full, sweet body; hops very restrained.
children.yearLabel: late 1700s–1800s Edinburgh ales; 'Wee Heavy' name from Fowler's

children.name: English Barley Wine
children.description: Very strong, complex, malt-rich ale with dark fruit, toffee and caramel and a balanced, often aged, warming finish.

origin.era: 18th–19th century; term popularised by Bass No. 1 (1870s)

children.yearLabel: 1872 (Bass No. 1 first called a barley wine)

parents.note: BJCP: a modern descendant of the strongest Burton Ales; Bass No. 1 was first called a barley wine in 1872.

children.name: American Barleywine
children.description: Very strong, hoppy, bitter barleywine with caramel/toffee malt matched by citrusy, piney American hops.

parents.note: BJCP: an adaptation of the English style using American ingredients and balance.

children.name: Wheatwine
children.description: Barleywine-strength ale with 50%+ wheat: bready, honeyed, fruity malt, softer texture and moderate hops; may be oak-aged.
hops: Any; often American (Cascade, Centennial) or noble

parents.note: A barleywine-strength beer built on wheat: 'barleywine's seductive cousin'.
Rubicon's first Winter Wheat Wine grew out of a (botched) batch of the brewpub's summer wheat beer.

children.name: American Strong Ale
children.description: Strong, full-flavoured, hop-forward ale with caramel malt and assertive bitterness; spans 'double red' and 'imperial amber' ales.

parents.note: BJCP: modern versions were developed as 'imperial' strength American amber/red ales (Double Reds).

children.name: Belgian & French Ales
children.description: Yeast-driven ales from Belgium and northern France: fruity esters, peppery phenols, high carbonation, often dry finishes and candi-sugar strength.

children.name: Abbey & Trappist Ales
children.description: Monastic-tradition ales built on Pilsner malt, candi sugar and expressive abbey yeast, from the light Single to the strong dark Quadrupel.

children.name: Trappist Single (Patersbier)
children.description: The monks' everyday table beer: pale, dry, hop-forward for a Belgian, with spicy-fruity yeast and a crisp, bitter finish.
children.yeast: Trappist/abbey ale yeast (e.g. Westmalle strain, WLP530/Wyeast 3787)

children.name: Belgian Dubbel
children.description: Deep amber to copper, malty-rich ale with dark-fruit (raisin, plum) esters, caramelized-sugar depth and a fairly dry finish.
children.yearLabel: 1922 (Westmalle double brown); monastic brown beer from 1856

adjuncts: Pale/white candi or table sugar (up to ~20%)
children.name: Belgian Tripel
children.description: Strong, pale gold, highly attenuated ale: spicy-fruity yeast (pepper, orange, banana), soft Pils malt, hidden alcohol and a dry, bitter finish.
children.yearLabel: 1930s (Witkap Pater c.1932; Westmalle Superbier 1934, named Tripel 1956)

parents.note: The name follows the strength ladder set by 'dubbel' (the brewery's third, strongest beer); a strong pale counterpart to Westmalle's dubbel.

children.name: Belgian Dark Strong Ale
children.description: Rich, strong dark ale with caramel, toffee, dark fruit and spice, warming but dangerously drinkable thanks to high attenuation.

topSellers.name: Rochefort 10
topSellers.brewery: Brasserie de Rochefort (Abbaye Notre-Dame de Saint-Rémy)

children.name: Quadrupel (Quad)
children.description: The strongest end of the abbey range: amber to dark brown, plush body, figs, raisins, dark sugar and warming alcohol. BJCP folds it into 26D Belgian Dark Strong Ale; the Brewers Association lists Belgian-Style Quadrupel on its own (stats here are BA 2026).

parents.note: BJCP: 'Quad' is the name used, mainly outside Belgium, for Belgian Dark Strong Ale; Quadrupel was a specific La Trappe beer.
La Trappe extended the dubbel/tripel strength naming to 'Quadrupel' in 1991.
The strongest rung of the abbeys' dark-beer ladder (e.g. Westvleteren 6/8/12; Chimay Red dubbel then Blue Grande Réserve).

children.name: Pale & Golden Ales
children.description: Secular Belgian ales from the session-strength amber Spéciale Belge to the blond and devilishly strong golden ales.

children.name: Belgian Pale Ale (Spéciale Belge)
children.description: Amber to copper, moderate-strength, drinkable ale with toasty-biscuity malt, gentle fruity esters, low phenols and moderate bitterness.
children.yeast: Fruity Belgian ale yeast with low phenols (De Koninck-type)

topSellers.name: Palm Spéciale Belge
topSellers.brewery: Palm Belgian Craft Brewers (Swinkels Family Brewers)

parents.note: BJCP: created after a 1904 competition for a regional specialty to compete with imported British ales and continental lagers.

children.name: Belgian Blond Ale
children.description: Golden, moderately strong, smooth and slightly sweet Pils-malt ale with light honeyed malt, soft fruity esters and a dry finish.

children.name: Belgian Golden Strong Ale
children.description: Pale, very dry, highly carbonated and deceptively strong: pear and citrus esters, peppery phenols, spicy hops and a crisp, effervescent finish.
children.yeast: Fruity Belgian ale yeast (Duvel/Moortgat strain, WLP570)
children.yearLabel: Duvel brewed from 1918/1923; modern pale form by 1970

parents.note: Moortgat's 1918 'Victory Ale' (Duvel from 1923) was modelled on British/Scotch ales using yeast from Scotland (McEwan's); BJCP says it was originally darker, achieving its pale form by the 1970s.

children.name: Belgian White
children.description: Spiced, hazy wheat ales from the Brabant countryside around Hoegaarden.

children.name: Witbier
children.description: Hazy, pale, refreshing wheat ale with coriander and orange-peel spice, a light lactic-citrus tartness and a creamy, effervescent body.
children.yearLabel: medieval (Leuven/Hoegaarden); extinct 1957, revived 1966 by Pierre Celis

children.name: Farmhouse Ales
children.description: Rustic, dry ales of Wallonia and French Flanders, historically brewed on farms for seasonal workers.

children.name: Saison
children.description: Dry, highly carbonated, fruity-spicy pale ale with peppery yeast, firm bitterness and a refreshing, bone-dry finish. BJCP recognises table (3.5–5%), standard (5–7%) and super (7–9.5%) strengths and pale (5–14 SRM) or dark (15–22 SRM) versions; the stats here are for standard pale.
children.yeast: Highly attenuative, peppery saison yeast (Dupont strain, WLP565/Wyeast 3724)

children.name: Super Saison
children.description: The strong end of BJCP 25B: same dry, peppery, fruity profile with more alcohol warmth and fuller malt.

topSellers.name: Saison Dupont Avec Les Bons Voeux

parents.note: BJCP: Dupont's stronger 'super saison' was first produced in 1954; strength variants of saison.

children.name: Grisette
children.description: Light, low-alcohol wheat-inclusive farmhouse ale, historically for Hainaut quarry and mine workers: crisp, dry, lemony and gently hopped. Not in BJCP or the BA 2026 guidelines; stats follow the BYO style profile, and modern commercial versions often run stronger (about 4-5.5%).

parents.note: BJCP: a well-known type of Saison popular with miners (session-strength, with wheat).

children.name: Bière de Garde
children.description: Malt-focused, cellar-aged French farmhouse ale in blonde, ambrée or brune versions: toasty, lightly caramel, clean and smooth with a dry finish.
children.yeast: Clean ale or lager yeast fermented cool, then long cold conditioning

children.name: Wheat Beers
children.description: Beers with a large share of malted wheat (or rye), from Bavarian banana-and-clove Weissbier to clean American wheat ales.

children.name: German Weissbier
children.description: Bavarian top-fermented wheat beers with at least 50% wheat malt and a weizen yeast giving banana esters and clove phenols.

children.name: Weissbier (Hefeweizen)
children.description: Pale, hazy, highly carbonated wheat beer with banana and clove from weizen yeast, soft bready wheat and a light, fluffy body.
children.yeast: Bavarian weizen yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan 68 / WLP300 / Wyeast 3068)

children.name: Kristallweizen
children.description: Filtered, brilliantly clear Weissbier: the same banana-clove yeast character, a bit crisper and lighter without the yeast. The BA lists South German-Style Kristal Weizen separately (straw to amber, stats here are BA 2026); BJCP includes filtered versions under 10A.
children.yeast: Bavarian weizen yeast, filtered before packaging

parents.note: Filtered version of Bavarian Weissbier; BJCP still treats filtered examples within 10A Weissbier.

children.name: Leichtes Weizen
children.description: Reduced-alcohol, lower-calorie Weissbier: lighter body with the same banana-clove yeast character in a softer form.

parents.note: Reduced-alcohol, lower-calorie version of Weissbier brewed by the big Bavarian wheat-beer brewers.

children.yearLabel: 16th century (Bavarian ducal wheat-beer privilege); modern Weissbier 1872 (Schneider); pale form popular from 1960s

children.name: Dunkles Weissbier
children.description: Dark Weissbier: banana-clove yeast over bready, toasty Munich and dark wheat malt with hints of caramel; light, creamy and refreshing.

origin.era: Traditional; older than pale Weissbier in common use

children.yearLabel: traditional dark Bavarian wheat beer; modern form from 1872 (Schneider)

parents.note: The older, darker form of the Bavarian wheat-beer tradition: old-fashioned Weissbier was often dark, and Schneider's 1872 amber Weisse began the modern era.

children.name: Weizenbock
children.description: Strong pale or dark wheat bock: rich bready/caramel malt, dark-fruit or banana esters, clove and warming alcohol. A freeze-concentrated 'Weizen-Eisbock' version exists (Schneider Aventinus Eisbock, ~12%), but it has no separate guideline.

parents.note: A Weissbier brewed to bock or doppelbock strength, created at Schneider Weisse in Munich.
Aventinus was conceived as a doppelbock-strength wheat beer, modelled on Munich's strong lagers.

children.name: Roggenbier
children.description: German rye beer brewed like a Dunkelweizen: grainy, spicy rye with banana-clove weizen yeast, a thick, creamy body and moderate brown color.

origin.era: Medieval rye beers; modern style 1988 (Schierlinger Roggen, later Thurn und Taxis / Paulaner)

parents.note: Essentially a Dunkles Weissbier brewed with malted rye instead of wheat, using weizen yeast.

children.name: American Wheat
children.description: Wheat beers fermented with clean ale or lager yeast, so no banana or clove.

adjuncts: Fruit or citrus in some versions
children.name: American Wheat Beer
children.description: Pale, refreshing wheat ale with clean fermentation, soft bready wheat and light-to-moderate American or noble hop character.
children.yeast: Clean American ale yeast (e.g. Chico/US-05) or lager yeast; no weizen yeast

parents.note: American craft adaptation of Weissbier with a cleaner yeast and more hops.

children.name: Wild & Sour
children.description: Beers made sour or funky by Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Brettanomyces or spontaneous fermentation, from Berliner Weisse to aged lambic.

children.name: German Sour Wheat
children.description: Light, tart wheat beers from northern and eastern Germany, soured with lactic acid bacteria.

children.name: Berliner Weisse
children.description: Very pale, low-alcohol, sharply sour and highly carbonated wheat beer: clean lactic tartness, bready wheat and a dry finish. Often served 'mit Schuss' with raspberry or woodruff syrup.
children.yeast: Top-fermenting ale yeast co-fermented with Lactobacillus (sometimes Brett)

topSellers.name: Berliner Kindl Weisse
topSellers.brewery: Berliner Kindl Schultheiss (Radeberger Gruppe / Oetker Group)

children.yearLabel: 16th–17th century (earliest Berlin record often given as 1572); "Champagne of the North" by 1809

children.name: Gose
children.description: Tart, lightly salty wheat beer with bright coriander-lemon spice, low bitterness and a refreshing, highly carbonated finish.
children.yeast: Clean ale yeast with Lactobacillus (kettle- or co-souring)

topSellers.name: Anderson Valley The Kimmie, The Yink & The Holy Gose

children.yearLabel: medieval (Goslar); in Leipzig by 1740; extinct 1966, revived 1980s

children.name: Flemish Sour Ales
children.description: West and East Flanders' aged, acetic-to-lactic sour ales with malt and fruit complexity.

children.name: Flanders Red Ale
children.description: Burgundy-red, wine-like sour ale: cherry, plum and red-currant fruit, lactic and gentle acetic sourness, oak and a balancing malt sweetness.
children.yeast: Ale yeast plus Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Brettanomyces and acetic bacteria; long oak foeder aging

parents.note: Rodenbach's ageing in large wooden vats and blending of old and young beer was borrowed from the English (vatted porter/stock ale) tradition.

children.name: Oud Bruin
children.description: Malty, brown East Flanders sour: caramel, toffee and dark fruit with a soft lactic (not acetic) tartness; aged in steel rather than oak.
children.yeast: Ale yeast with Lactobacillus (and Sacch); aged

children.name: Lambic Family
children.description: Spontaneously fermented wheat beers of the Senne valley and Pajottenland around Brussels, aged in oak and blended.

children.name: Lambic
children.description: Unblended, often still, spontaneously fermented wheat beer: sour, funky (barnyard, hay, horse blanket), with lemony and oak notes and almost no hop bitterness.
hops: Aged (3+ years) low-alpha hops, used as preservative
children.yeast: Spontaneous fermentation (coolship): Sacch, Brettanomyces, Lactobacillus, Pediococcus and others
children.yearLabel: at least 16th century (Senne valley farmhouse tradition)

children.name: Gueuze
children.description: Blend of 1-, 2- and 3-year-old lambics refermented in the bottle: sparkling, intensely sour and complex with funk, citrus, oak and a bone-dry finish. Sweetened commercial gueuzes (Belle-Vue, Mort Subite) outsell the traditional 'oude' versions.
children.yeast: Spontaneous mixed fermentation; bottle refermentation from young lambic
children.yearLabel: 1830s–40s first bottled gueuze; blended champagne-bottle form later 1800s

parents.note: Blend of young and old lambic, bottle-conditioned; same basic history as lambic.

children.name: Faro
children.description: Lambic sweetened with brown or candi sugar (historically blended with weaker beer): sweet-sour, caramel and light funk. BJCP only mentions it in the 23D Lambic comments and gives no separate stats; ranges here are the 23D numbers widened to cover commercial versions (about 4-5%).
children.yeast: Spontaneous fermentation (lambic base); modern bottled versions pasteurised

parents.note: Brussels café beer: lambic blended with weaker meerts and sweetened with sugar.

adjuncts: Whole fruit: peach, apricot, blackcurrant, grape and others
children.name: Fruit Lambic
children.description: Lambic or gueuze refermented on whole fruit: the fruit leads, over a sour, funky, dry lambic base. Modern mass-market versions are sweetened and pasteurised.

children.name: Kriek
children.description: Cherry lambic, traditionally made with sour Schaerbeek cherries: tart cherry and almond-like pit over a funky, dry lambic base. BJCP 23F color (3-7 SRM) varies with the fruit, so real examples are often deep red.
children.yearLabel: 19th-century tradition; documented recipes by c. 1900 (Schaerbeek cherries)

parents.note: Sour Schaerbeek cherries macerated in lambic, traditionally by the blender or publican.

children.name: Framboise
children.description: Raspberry lambic: vivid raspberry aroma and pink-red color with sour, funky lambic character. BJCP 23F color (3-7 SRM) varies with the fruit, so real examples are often deep red.

parents.note: Raspberries macerated in lambic, following the fruit-lambic tradition.

children.yearLabel: c. 1900 (kriek first); other fruits 20th century; sweetened versions from 1970s

parents.note: Fruit added to lambic by blenders and publicans to vary café offerings.
BJCP: "same basic history as Gueuze", with fruit (and in modern versions sugar) added to the blend.

children.name: American Wild & Mixed Fermentation
children.description: Modern wild ales, mostly American, using Brett, Lacto, Pedio or house mixed cultures, often barrel-aged and fruited. BJCP gives no fixed vital statistics; they vary with the base beer.

children.name: American Wild Ale
children.description: Umbrella for American-made sour and funky ales: any base beer fermented or aged with wild yeast and/or bacteria, often in oak, with fruit, funk and acidity in any balance. BJCP gives no vital statistics (variable by base style); the ranges shown are deliberately broad.
malts: Specialty malts as for base style
hops: Low-alpha or aged hops (hops inhibit Lacto)
children.yeast: House mixed cultures: Sacch with Brett, Lactobacillus and/or Pediococcus; coolship spontaneous in some

children.name: Brett Beer
children.description: Any base beer fermented or finished with Brettanomyces but no bacteria: tropical, stone-fruit or barnyard funk, very dry, not intentionally sour. BJCP gives no vital statistics (variable by base style); the ranges shown are deliberately broad.
children.yeast: Brettanomyces (100% Brett or Sacch primary + Brett); no Lacto/Pedio

parents.note: American wild-ale subtype fermented with Brettanomyces, inspired by Belgian wild ales and historical Brett-aged English beers.

children.name: Mixed-Fermentation Sour Beer
children.description: Sour, funky beer from any combination of Sacch, Brett, Lacto and Pedio, often oak-aged: layered acidity, fruity esters and Brett complexity. BJCP gives no vital statistics (variable by base style); the ranges shown are deliberately broad.
children.yeast: Mixed culture: Sacch + Brettanomyces + Lactobacillus + Pediococcus

parents.note: Subcategory of American wild ale using mixed Sacch/Brett/bacteria cultures.
Modern American interpretations of Belgian sour ales.
Modern American interpretations of Belgian sour ales.

children.name: Wild Specialty Beer
children.description: A Brett, mixed-fermentation or sour beer with fruit, herbs, spices or distinctive wood/barrel character (e.g. wine or spirit barrels). BJCP gives no vital statistics (variable by base style); the ranges shown are deliberately broad.

parents.note: American wild ale with fruit, spice, wood or other specialty additions.
Fruited wild ales are interpretations of fruited Belgian wild ales.

children.yearLabel: late 1990s–2000s (New Belgium, Russian River, Jolly Pumpkin)

parents.note: Modern American interpretations of, or experiments inspired by, Belgian wild ales.
Barrel-aged sour reds/browns such as New Belgium La Folie follow the Flemish sour model.

children.name: Kettle & Fruited Sours
children.description: Fast, clean lactic sours (kettle-soured or co-fermented), usually loaded with fruit, from the US craft scene and Brazil.

adjuncts: Fruit puree (passion fruit, raspberry, mango, guava)
children.name: Fruited Kettle Sour
children.description: Clean, bright lactic sour (no Brett funk) on a pale or wheat base, heavily fruited; color and flavor follow the fruit. The BA lists it as American-Style Fruited Sour Ale but says all stats "may vary widely"; ABV/IBU here follow the unfruited base, BJCP 28D Straight Sour Beer, with a broad color range for the fruit.
children.yeast: Kettle souring with Lactobacillus, then clean ale yeast (or lactic-producing yeast such as Philly Sour)

parents.note: Kettle souring derives from the Francke acidification process developed to speed up Berliner Weisse production.
BJCP notes Gose is often used as a base for fruited sour beers.

adjuncts: Fresh fruit (araçá, jabuticaba, peach, passion fruit, guava, tangerine)
children.name: Catharina Sour
children.description: Brazilian light, refreshing wheat-based kettle sour with fresh (often tropical) fruit: clean lactic tartness, no perceptible bitterness, no Brett, fruit-forward and dry. BJCP 2021 Appendix B local style X4.
children.yeast: Kettle souring with Lactobacillus, then clean ale yeast

topSellers.name: Blumenau Catharina Sour Sun of a Peach (Pêssego)

parents.note: "Like a stronger Berliner Weisse, but with fresh fruit and no Brett."
Fruited wheat beer made with the Lacto kettle-sour technique and fresh, often tropical, fruit.

children.name: Grape Ales
children.description: Beer-wine hybrids fermented with grape must. Placed here because many Italian Grape Ales show light tartness or wild character; the international 29D Grape Ale sits with fruit beers in the Specialty family.

adjuncts: Grape must or sapa (cooked must), red or white varieties
children.name: Italian Grape Ale
children.description: Italian ale fermented with grape must or grapes (up to ~40% of the grist): vinous grape and fruit aromas, often light tartness or a low wild character, dry and highly carbonated. BJCP 2021 Appendix B local style X3 (stats here); non-Italian versions go in 29D Grape Ale, which has narrower stats (6-8.5% ABV, 4-8 SRM).
hops: Low-alpha Old World hops (German or English), used sparingly
children.yeast: Neutral ale yeast (most common) or fruity/spicy Belgian/English strains; some with wild yeast or wine yeast

children.name: Lagers
children.description: Bottom-fermented beers that are cold-fermented and cold-conditioned (lagered), giving a clean, crisp profile. They range from ice-cold light lagers to strong Bavarian bocks.

children.name: Light & International Pale Lagers
children.description: Mass-market pale lagers: very pale, highly carbonated, low bitterness, often brewed with rice or corn.

children.name: American Light Lager
children.description: Very pale, very light-bodied, highly carbonated lager with minimal malt and hop flavor and a crisp, dry finish; built to be served ice cold. Michelob Ultra became the No. 1 US beer by volume in 2025 (Circana, 52 weeks to Sept. 2025), overtaking Modelo Especial; Bud Light lost the top spot in 2023.
children.yeast: Clean American lager yeast; added enzymes for very high attenuation

parents.note: Diet-conscious, lower-calorie version of the standard American lager.

children.name: American Lager
children.description: Very pale, highly carbonated, crisp and clean adjunct lager with a neutral grainy palate and low bitterness; slightly fuller than light lager.
children.yearLabel: 1870s (adjunct pale lagers, e.g. Budweiser 1876); modern form after 1933

parents.note: Evolved from Pre-Prohibition Lager after Prohibition and WWII as surviving breweries consolidated.

children.name: International Pale Lager
children.description: Highly attenuated pale lager with a little more body and hop bitterness than American lager; the worldwide mass-market "premium lager".

parents.note: Developed outside the US as imitations of American-style lagers (and in the US as premium versions of them).
Also developed as a more accessible, drier, less bitter version of Pilsner-type beer.

children.name: Mexican Lager
children.description: Clean, crisp, very pale lager with a light grainy-corn sweetness and low hop character; often served with lime. The Brewers Association lists Mexican-Style Light, Pale, Amber and Dark Lager separately; stats shown are BA Mexican-Style Pale Lager. BJCP has no separate style (Corona Extra is a BJCP 2A example).

topSellers.name: Corona Extra
topSellers.brewery: Grupo Modelo (AB InBev; Constellation Brands in US)

topSellers.name: Modelo Especial
topSellers.brewery: Grupo Modelo (AB InBev; Constellation Brands in US)

topSellers.name: Pacifico
topSellers.brewery: Grupo Modelo (AB InBev; Constellation Brands in US)

parents.note: Mexican lager brewing was founded by Austrian and German immigrant brewers such as Santiago Graf, who brought Vienna lager.
Pale Mexican lagers (Corona and others) are BJCP 2A International Pale Lagers, the accessible Pilsner/American type.

children.name: Rice Lager
children.description: Very pale, brilliantly clear, dry ("karakuchi") lager in which rice (at least 15% of the grist under BA rules) lightens the body and sharpens the finish; hops stay integrated rather than dominant. Stats are the BA "Rice Lager" guideline; BJCP has no separate style (Asahi Super Dry is a BJCP 2A example).

origin.era: Rice in lagers since 1800s; Asahi Super Dry 1987

children.yearLabel: rice adjunct lagers since late 1800s; dry style 1987 (Asahi Super Dry)

parents.note: Asahi Super Dry and similar rice lagers are classic BJCP 2A International Pale Lager examples.

children.name: American Malt Liquor
children.description: Strong, very pale, high-adjunct lager with a sweet corn-sugar character, minimal hops and noticeable alcohol warmth. BA notes that some are barely stronger than American lager while others approach bock strength; market leader Steel Reserve 211 (8.1%) sits above the BA 6.3-7.6% range.

parents.note: Stronger, high-adjunct variant of American mass-market lager.

children.name: German Pale Lagers
children.description: Malt-led pale lagers from Bavaria and northern Germany: soft grainy Pils malt and restrained noble hops.

children.name: Munich Helles
children.description: Clean, malty, gold lager with a smooth grainy-sweet Pils malt flavor, soft finish and just enough noble-hop bitterness for balance.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Created in Munich to compete with pale Pilsner-type beers.

children.name: Festbier
children.description: Golden, smooth, rich-but-clean lager served at the Munich Oktoberfest since the 1970s; fuller than Helles with a bready Pils-malt depth.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Paulaner developed a lighter, golden, more drinkable version of the traditional Oktoberfest Märzen.

children.name: German Helles Exportbier (Dortmunder Export)
children.description: Pale, well-balanced, smooth lager that is a bit stronger than Helles and bolder in body and bitterness, with a minerally dry finish from Dortmund water.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Developed in Dortmund in response to pale Pilsner-type beers.

children.name: Kellerbier
children.description: Unfiltered, unpasteurized German lager traditionally served young from the lagering vessel; may be a Helles, Pils, Märzen or Dunkel base and is a little richer, more rustic and often slightly hazier than the filtered base style. BJCP and BA both give stats "same as / varies with base style"; the ranges shown are an approximate envelope spanning Pils/Helles to Märzen bases.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70); left unfiltered
children.yearLabel: 1800s (Franconian cellar lagers); now a broad term for unfiltered lager

children.name: German Leichtbier
children.description: Pale, highly attenuated, light-bodied German lager with lower alcohol and calories than standard beers but still noticeable malt and noble-hop flavor.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Modern versions are based on popular American light lagers, aimed at health-conscious drinkers.

children.name: Pilsners & Hoppy Pale Lagers
children.description: Hop-forward pale lagers descended from the 1842 Pilsen original, plus modern dry-hopped and New World versions.

children.name: German Pils
children.description: Light gold, crisp, dry and bitter lager with a flowery-spicy noble hop aroma and a clean grainy malt base.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Adapted from Czech Pilsner to harder German water and German hop varieties.

children.name: Czech Premium Pale Lager (Bohemian Pilsner)
children.description: Rich, complex golden lager with a bready Czech-malt depth, soft rounded Saaz bitterness, spicy hop aroma and often a touch of diacetyl.
children.yeast: Czech lager yeast (e.g. Pilsen H strain / WLP800)

parents.note: Bavarian brewer Josef Groll brought Bavarian lager yeast and bottom fermentation to Plzeň, combined with English pale-malting techniques.

children.name: Czech Pale Lager (Světlé výčepní)
children.description: Light, rich, refreshing and hoppy everyday Czech draft lager (about 10° Plato) with a bready malt flavor and soft Saaz bitterness.

parents.note: Groll brewed a smaller výčepní alongside the ležák in 1842–3; the lighter sibling of the original Pilsner.

children.name: Italian Pilsner
children.description: A German-style Pils that is dry-hopped with noble hops, giving an intense floral-herbal aroma over a crisp, dry, pale base. Named after Birrificio Italiano Tipopils (1996). Stats are the BA "Italian-Style Pilsener" guideline; BJCP has no separate style (Tipopils is a 34B Mixed-Style example).
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Agostino Arioli, trained in German breweries, set out to brew a northern German-style Pils and dry-hopped it with noble hops.

children.name: New Zealand Pilsner
children.description: Pale, dry, crisp lager-like beer showcasing New Zealand hops with tropical, white-wine and lime notes and a firm clean bitterness.
children.yeast: Clean lager yeast or very neutral ale yeast

parents.note: Emerson's described its Pilsner as a take on the Czech/German style, originally hopped with Saaz D (now Riwaka).
Emerson's described its Pilsner as a take on the Czech/German style, reinterpreted with New Zealand hops.

children.name: India Pale Lager (IPL)
children.description: A crisp, clean lager hopped like an American IPA, with heavy late and dry hopping (citrus, tropical, pine) over a dry, lightly malty base. Stats are the BA "American-Style India Pale Lager" guideline; BJCP has no IPL style and sends these to 34B Mixed-Style (Hoponius Union is a 34B example). "Cold IPA" is a closely related offshoot.

parents.note: A pale lager hopped like an American IPA, fermented cold and lagered.

children.name: Amber Lagers
children.description: Toasty, malt-forward lagers built on Vienna and Munich malts, from amber-orange to copper.

children.name: Vienna Lager
children.description: Moderately strong, reddish-amber lager with a soft, elegant toasty Vienna-malt character, moderate bitterness and a dry finish.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Dreher applied Bavarian bottom fermentation (learned with Sedlmayr at Spaten, Munich) to paler, English-style kilned malt.

children.name: Märzen (Oktoberfest)
children.description: Elegant, malty, amber-orange to copper German lager with a rich, toasty-bready Munich/Vienna malt depth and a dry, clean finish; the pre-1990 Oktoberfest beer.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: Spaten's 1841 lager was contemporaneous with Dreher's; Josef Sedlmayr's 1872 Oktoberfest Märzen was brewed on the Vienna template.
The Märzen name is older than 1841: early March-brewed Bavarian lagers were dark brown, stored in cellars over summer.

children.name: International Amber Lager
children.description: Smooth, easy-drinking amber mass-market lager with mild caramel/toast malt flavor and low bitterness; may use adjuncts.

parents.note: Generally an amber adaptation of mass-market International Pale Lager.

children.name: Czech Amber Lager (Polotmavé)
children.description: Malt-driven amber to copper Czech lager with caramel, toast and bready notes, balanced by spicy Saaz hops; may be fuller or drier depending on brewery.

parents.note: A Vienna-style lager that has continued to be brewed in the Czech lands.

children.name: Dark Lagers
children.description: Brown to black lagers, from bready-malty Munich Dunkel to roasty-dry Schwarzbier.

children.name: Munich Dunkel
children.description: Deep copper to dark brown Bavarian lager with a rich, bready-toasty Munich-malt flavor, hints of chocolate or nuts, and a smooth, clean finish.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)
children.yearLabel: 16th century Bavarian brown lager (1553 summer-brewing ban); modern Dunkel 1830s (Spaten)

children.name: Schwarzbier
children.description: Very dark, dry German black lager with a soft roast and chocolate character, no harsh burnt flavors, and a crisp lager finish.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

children.name: Czech Dark Lager (Tmavé)
children.description: Rich, dark, malty Czech lager whose roast ranges from barely noticeable to prominent, with caramel and bready notes and a spicy Czech-hop balance.
children.yearLabel: U Fleků brewing since 1499; dark lager form 1800s

children.name: International Dark Lager
children.description: Dark, smooth, easy-drinking mass-market lager with light caramel and roast, low bitterness and a sweetish finish; may use adjuncts and coloring.
malts: Light use of dark roasted malt

topSellers.name: Negra Modelo
topSellers.brewery: Grupo Modelo (AB InBev; Constellation Brands in US)

parents.note: Darker, coloured or sweetened versions of International Pale Lager from the same industrial breweries.
Also brewed as a more accessible and cheaper version of traditional dark lagers.

children.name: Bocks
children.description: Strong German lagers, from the pale spring Maibock up to freeze-concentrated Eisbock.

children.name: Helles Bock (Maibock)
children.description: Relatively pale, strong, malty German lager with a bready-toasty Pils/Munich malt character, more hop presence than other bocks, and a dry finish.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)

parents.note: A fairly recent pale development within the bock family.
BJCP: can be seen as a Helles or Festbier brewed to bock strength.

children.name: Dunkles Bock
children.description: Dark, strong, malty lager with a rich, toasty Munich/Vienna malt character, melanoidin depth and very little hop flavor.
malts: Tiny % dark roasted malt for color
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)
children.yearLabel: 14th century (Einbeck, Hanseatic export); recreated in Munich from the 1600s

children.name: Doppelbock
children.description: Very strong, rich, malty lager, either golden or (more often) dark, with deep bready-toasty malt, dark-fruit hints, low bitterness and alcohol warmth. Names traditionally end in "-ator".
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70)
children.yearLabel: 1600s–1700s (Paulaner monks, Munich; strong Lenten beer from 1651, later "Salvator")

parents.note: Munich monks' stronger "liquid bread" member of the Bock family.

children.name: Eisbock
children.description: Full-bodied, very strong, dark lager made by freezing a doppelbock and removing ice, which concentrates its malt, dark-fruit and alcohol.
children.yeast: Clean German lager yeast (e.g. Weihenstephan W-34/70); then freeze-concentrated

parents.note: Made by freezing a strong bock or doppelbock and removing ice to concentrate it.

children.name: Hybrid Beers
children.description: Beers that cross ale and lager methods: ales fermented cool and lagered, or lager yeast fermented warm.

children.name: German Hybrids (Obergärig Lagerbier)
children.description: Top-fermented ales from the Rhineland that are cold-conditioned like lagers: Kölsch in Cologne and Altbier in Düsseldorf.

children.name: Kölsch
children.description: Clean, crisp, delicately balanced pale ale from Cologne with a soft grainy-honey malt, faint fruity esters, subtle noble hops and a dry, lagered finish. "Kölsch" is a protected appellation (Kölsch Konvention, 1986), so American versions are labeled "Kölsch-style".
children.yeast: Attenuative, clean Kölsch ale yeast fermented cool (~15 °C), then cold-lagered

parents.note: Cologne's top-fermenting brewers developed Kölsch in the late 1800s as an alternative to pale lagers.

children.name: Altbier
children.description: Well-balanced, bitter yet malty, clean copper-brown ale from Düsseldorf with a firm, lasting bitterness, rich grainy-toasty malt and a dry, lagered finish.
malts: Touch of chocolate/black malt or roasted wheat
children.yeast: Clean, highly attenuative Altbier ale yeast (e.g. WLP036 / Wyeast 1007), fermented cool then cold-conditioned

children.name: Sticke Alt
children.description: A "secret" seasonal Altbier from Düsseldorf's brewpubs. It is stronger, darker, maltier and more heavily hopped than standard Alt, and often dry-hopped. Uerige also brews a ~8.5% Doppelsticke. The ranges are approximate, because neither BJCP nor BA defines this style.

parents.note: Stronger, hoppier "secret" seasonal version of Düsseldorf Altbier.

children.name: American Hybrids
children.description: American beers that mix ale and lager techniques: lager yeast at ale temperatures (steam beer), or ales built to compete with lagers (cream ale).

children.name: Cream Ale
children.description: Clean, well-attenuated, highly carbonated pale ale (sometimes blended with lager) with a light corn sweetness and low bitterness. It was created as an ale brewer's answer to light lager.
children.yeast: Clean American ale yeast, or ale/lager blend, fermented cool

topSellers.name: Genesee Cream Ale
topSellers.brewery: Genesee Brewing (North American Breweries; ex-FIFCO USA)

children.yearLabel: second half of the 1800s; survived Prohibition

parents.note: A sparkling ale brewed to compete with the lagers of the US Northeast, Mid-Atlantic and Midwest.

children.name: California Common (Steam Beer)
children.description: Toasty, caramelly amber beer with firm bitterness and rustic, minty-woody Northern Brewer hops, fermented with lager yeast at warm ale temperatures. "Steam Beer" is an Anchor trademark. The archetype, Anchor Steam, has been out of production since Anchor Brewing closed in July 2023; Chobani founder Hamdi Ulukaya bought the brewery in May 2024, but brewing had not resumed as of late 2026.
children.yeast: Warm-tolerant lager yeast fermented at 55-60 °F (e.g. WLP810 San Francisco Lager)
children.yearLabel: Gold Rush era (1850s steam beer); Anchor revival 1971

children.name: Specialty Beers
children.description: Beers defined by an added ingredient or process (smoke, wood, fruit, spice, alternative grains or sugars) laid on top of a base style, plus gluten-free, non-alcoholic and experimental beers.

children.name: Smoked Beers
children.description: Beers made with smoked malt, from Bamberg's beechwood Rauchbier to any style given a smoke accent.

children.name: Rauchbier
children.description: Bamberg-style amber Märzen brewed with beechwood-smoked malt: a toasty, malty lager with a smoky (bacon, campfire) character from mild to intense.
children.yearLabel: medieval smoked-malt roots (Schlenkerla); Märzen-based Rauchbier after 1841

parents.note: Bamberg smoked lager built on a Märzen base; BJCP says the style must have developed after Märzen.

children.name: Classic Style Smoked Beer
children.description: A classic base style such as porter, bock or Helles brewed with smoked malt (beech, oak, alder, fruitwood and others) so the smoke blends harmoniously with the base beer. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

origin.era: Smoked malt pre-1700s; modern revival 1980s+ (e.g. Alaskan Smoked Porter 1988)

malts: Smoked malt (beech, oak, alder, cherry, peat-free)
children.yearLabel: smoked malt traditional; modern revival 1980s+ (Alaskan Smoked Porter 1988)

parents.note: Craft brewers adapted the German smoked-malt tradition (Rauchbier and smoked Bock, Weissbier, Helles and more) to many base styles.

children.name: Specialty Smoked Beer
children.description: A smoked beer built on a base style and also given other specialty ingredients such as fruit, spice, honey, vanilla or barrel aging. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

topSellers.name: Stone Smoked Porter with Vanilla Bean
topSellers.brewery: Stone Brewing (Firestone Walker / Duvel Moortgat USA since 2026)

children.name: Wood & Barrel-Aged Beers
children.description: Beers aged in wood or on wood: neutral oak, or barrels that previously held spirits or wine.

children.name: Wood-Aged Beer
children.description: A base beer aged in wooden barrels or on oak/other wood without a previous alcohol character, picking up vanilla, toast, coconut, caramel or tannin. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

origin.era: Wooden casks were historical norm; modern deliberate wood character 1990s+

adjuncts: Oak chips, staves, spirals or cubes
children.yearLabel: wooden casks traditional; deliberate wood character 1990s+

children.name: Specialty Wood-Aged Beer (Barrel-Aged)
children.description: A beer aged in barrels that previously held spirits or wine, such as bourbon, rum or port. Imperial stouts in bourbon barrels are the archetype, with vanilla, oak, caramel and boozy-spirit notes. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.
malts: Per base style (often imperial stout / barleywine grists)

parents.note: Wood ageing with spirit, wine or other previous barrel contents; BJCP gives it the same history as 33A.

children.name: Fruit Beers
children.description: Non-sour beers built around fruit, from shandies and fruit wheats to grape-must ales. Fruited lambics, sours and Italian Grape Ale belong to Wild & Sour.

children.name: Fruit Beer
children.description: A base beer with one or more fruits added, where the fruit flavor is clearly noticeable yet balanced with the beer. Radlers and shandies are commercial cousins. BJCP gives no numbers (stats vary with the base style); the ranges shown are the BA "American-Style Fruit Beer" guideline (SRM 5-50 "or color of fruit").

origin.era: Ancient roots; modern US fruit beers 1980s+

malts: Per base style (often pale, wheat or light lager bases)
adjuncts: Fruit, purée, juice or concentrate (e.g. raspberry, cherry, citrus, watermelon)
children.yearLabel: ancient roots; modern craft fruit beers 1980s+

children.name: Fruit and Spice Beer
children.description: A beer with both fruit and spices, herbs or vegetables, which blend with each other and the base beer. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

children.name: Grape Ale
children.description: BJCP 2021's general grape-must category: a relatively neutral pale beer co-fermented with grape must (typically 15-20% of the grist) for a dry, sparkling-wine-like character; not sour or Brett-funky. It grew out of Italian Grape Ale, which BJCP keeps as a separate local style (X3, broader ranges) and which this dataset lists under Wild & Sour.
children.yeast: Fruity-spicy ale yeast or neutral/wine yeast

parents.note: The Italian Grape Ale, published by BJCP in 2015, inspired many local variations in other countries.

children.name: Spice, Herb & Flavored Beers
children.description: Beers flavored with spices, herbs, vegetables, chiles, coffee, chocolate or honey, including the seasonal pumpkin and winter beers.

children.name: Spice, Herb, or Vegetable Beer
children.description: A base beer showcasing spices, herbs or vegetables (heather, ginger, jasmine, botanicals) in harmony with the underlying style. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

children.name: Pumpkin / Autumn Seasonal Beer
children.description: An amber to copper, malty seasonal beer with "pumpkin pie" spices (cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice, clove, ginger), often with pumpkin or squash and brown sugar or molasses. BJCP 30B gives no numbers; the ranges shown are the BA "Pumpkin Spice Beer" guideline (BA also lists an unspiced Pumpkin/Squash Beer).
children.yearLabel: 1985 (Buffalo Bill's Pumpkin Ale); colonial pumpkin beers earlier

children.name: Winter Seasonal Beer
children.description: A stronger, darker, warming holiday beer with Christmas spices, citrus peel or dried fruit, and malty, caramel-rich depth. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

origin.era: Traditional winter ales; Anchor Christmas Ale 1975

children.yeast: Ale or lager yeast per base
children.yearLabel: traditional winter ales; Anchor Our Special Ale 1975

parents.note: British winter warmers such as Young's Winter Warmer are survivors of the old Burton Ale style.

children.name: Chile Beer
children.description: A beer flavored with chile peppers, with green-vegetal or fruity pepper flavor and heat ranging from subtle to fiery. BA calls it "Chili Pepper Beer". Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.
malts: Per base style (often light lager, pale ale or stout)
adjuncts: Chile peppers (jalapeño, habanero, serrano, chipotle, ghost)

topSellers.name: Xocoveza
topSellers.brewery: Stone Brewing (Firestone Walker / Duvel Moortgat USA since 2026)

children.name: Coffee Beer
children.description: A beer, most often a stout or porter, flavored with coffee beans or cold brew so that roast-coffee aroma and flavor stand out. Pale "golden coffee" versions also exist. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.
malts: Per base style (often roasted barley, chocolate malt, oats)
adjuncts: Coffee (whole bean, cold brew or espresso)

children.name: Chocolate Beer
children.description: A beer, usually dark, flavored with chocolate, cocoa or cacao nibs for a clear chocolate character beyond what dark malts provide. BA calls it "Chocolate or Cocoa Beer". Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

children.name: Honey Beer
children.description: A beer brewed with honey so that its floral, sweet-aromatic honey character is noticeable, often with a drier body because honey ferments out completely. BJCP files it under 31B Alternative Sugar. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.
children.yeast: Ale or lager yeast per base
adjuncts: Honey (clover, orange blossom, heather and others)

children.name: Alternative & Other Specialty
children.description: Beers defined by alternative ingredients or processes: other grains and sugars, gluten-free, non-alcoholic and experimental.

children.name: Alternative Grain Beer
children.description: A base style brewed with a noticeable share of a non-standard grain, such as rye, buckwheat, spelt, millet, sorghum or rice, which adds its own flavor and texture. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.
malts: Alternative grain (rye, spelt, buckwheat, oats, millet, sorghum)

children.name: Alternative Sugar Beer
children.description: A base beer with a noticeable sugar adjunct, such as maple syrup, molasses, piloncillo, candi syrup or agave, that adds flavor beyond fermentables. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

children.name: Gluten-Free Beer
children.description: A beer made only from gluten-free ingredients (sorghum, millet, buckwheat, rice, corn and others) and often imitating a classic style. BA puts gluten-reduced barley beers in their base style, not here. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.
hops: Per target style (Cascade, Saaz and others)

children.name: Non-Alcoholic Beer
children.description: A beer that imitates any style with less than 0.5% ABV, made by dealcoholization, arrested or limited fermentation, or special yeast; quality has risen sharply since 2018. BA calls it "Non-Alcohol Malt Beverage".
hops: Per target style (often heavy late hopping for NA IPAs)
children.yeast: Maltose-negative yeast, arrested fermentation, or dealcoholized after normal fermentation

children.name: Experimental Beer
children.description: A catch-all for beers that fit no other style: unusual ingredients, processes or fermentation, including "extreme" freeze-concentrated or ancient-recipe beers. Stats vary with the base style. The ranges shown are a typical envelope, not a guideline limit.

children.name: Historical & Regional
children.description: Extinct, revived and living folk beers, from medieval German and Dutch ales to Nordic farmhouse brews and indigenous beers around the world.

children.name: German & Central European Historical
children.description: Revived or surviving old-world styles from Germany, Poland and the Low Countries: smoked and sour wheat beers, oat beers, steam and stone beers.

children.name: Lichtenhainer
children.description: A sour, smoked, low-gravity wheat beer from Thuringia. It is complex yet refreshing, with moderate lactic tartness, a light smoke and very low bitterness, much like a pre-1840 Berliner Weisse.

children.name: Piwo Grodziskie (Grätzer)
children.description: A low-gravity, highly carbonated, bitter Polish wheat beer made from oak-smoked wheat malt. It has a clean fermentation and no sourness. It is known in German as Grätzer and nicknamed "Polish champagne".
children.yeast: Clean, attenuative ale yeast (historically a multi-strain top-fermenter); not Weizen yeast

children.name: Broyhan
children.description: A pale, top-fermented wheat-and-barley beer from Hanover, first brewed by Cord Broyhan in 1526 and made until about 1919, with a light, slightly sweet-sour character. Recent revivals sometimes add botanicals. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.
children.yeast: Top-fermenting ale yeast, sometimes with lactic souring

children.name: Adambier
children.description: A strong, dark, hoppy old Dortmund ale, traditionally long-aged in wood and sometimes slightly sour or lightly smoky, with toast, caramel and dark-fruit notes. Stats are the BA "Adambier" guideline.

origin.era: Medieval roots; died out by mid-1900s; revived 1994 (Hair of the Dog)

children.yearLabel: pre-lager Dortmund ale (documented 1800s); revived 1994 (Hair of the Dog)

children.name: Dampfbier
children.description: A Bavarian Forest "steam beer": an amber, all-barley ale fermented warm with Weizen-type yeast, giving fruity-phenolic notes. It was named for the bubbling ("steaming") fermentation. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.
children.yeast: Bavarian Weizen ale yeast fermented warm

children.name: Zoigl
children.description: An unfiltered, young, amber-gold lager brewed in the communal brewhouses (Kommunbrauhäuser) of the Upper Palatinate and served only in the brewers' own Zoiglstuben, which open in rotation on a published calendar, signaled by a hanging six-pointed star. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.

origin.country: Germany (Upper Palatinate: Windischeschenbach, Neuhaus, Falkenberg, Mitterteich, Eslarn)

children.yeast: Bottom-fermenting lager yeast, cool-fermented in household cellars

children.name: Steinbier
children.description: A "stone beer" boiled by dropping red-hot greywacke or granite stones into the wort. The stones caramelize sugars, and they are then added back during maturation for a smoky-caramel, toffee character. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.

origin.era: Pre-modern (no metal kettles); revived 1982 by Rauchenfels (since retired), today Leikeim and Hofstetten

children.name: Mumme (Brunswick Mum)
children.description: A thick, near-black, sweet, strong ale from Braunschweig that was exported widely by sea in the 1500s-1700s. Today it survives mainly as a non-alcoholic malt extract; Nettelbeck's revived Mumme beer has reportedly ended production, and the name lives on in Scandinavian Christmas beers. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.
adjuncts: Historically herbs and spices (fir/birch tips in some recipes)

children.name: Kuit / Kuyt / Koyt
children.description: A medieval Dutch oat beer: gold to copper, grainy-bready, lightly hopped and sometimes gruit-spiced. Under BA rules the grist is at least 45% oats and 20% wheat; stats are the BA "Dutch-Style Kuit, Kuyt or Koyt" guideline (Jopen Koyt, at 8.5%, is stronger than the BA range).
adjuncts: Optional gruit herbs (bog myrtle and others)

children.name: Nordic & Baltic Farmhouse Ales
children.description: Raw-ale traditions from Finland, Gotland, Norway and Estonia: juniper, home-smoked malt, farmhouse yeast (kveik) and often no boil.

children.name: Sahti
children.description: A sweet, heavy, strong Finnish farmhouse ale, usually with rye and juniper, a banana-clove yeast character and little or no hops. The wort is often unboiled and filtered through juniper twigs in a kuurna trough.

origin.era: At least 500 years; EU TSG protected 2002

children.yeast: Finnish baker's yeast, warm and fast (Weizen yeast as substitute)
children.yearLabel: at least 500 years (Finnish farmhouse tradition); EU TSG 2002

children.name: Gotlandsdricka
children.description: A Gotland (Sweden) farmhouse ale brewed with birch-smoked malt and juniper-infused water. It is smoky, piney-resinous and sweetish, sometimes with honey, and fermented with baker's or farmhouse yeast. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.
children.yearLabel: medieval / Viking-age roots (approx.); living farmhouse tradition

children.name: Stjørdalsøl
children.description: A Norwegian farmhouse ale from the Stjørdal valley, made from home-malted barley kilned in smoke-filled "såinnhus" kilns. It is intensely smoky, juniper-tinged and often fermented with kveik. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.

origin.era: Living farmhouse tradition (more than 400 home brewers)

children.name: Koduõlu
children.description: An Estonian farmhouse ("home") ale, strongest on Saaremaa and Muhu islands: unboiled, naturally carbonated, hazy, sweetish and juniper-scented, with fruity, rustic farmhouse-yeast character; usually 6-9% ABV. Almost all is home-brewed; Pihtla on Saaremaa is the main commercial producer. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.

children.name: Anglo-American Historical
children.description: Extinct or nearly extinct styles from 1800s Britain and pre-Prohibition America.

children.name: Kentucky Common
children.description: A clean, dry, refreshing, slightly malty dark saloon beer from Louisville. It is mild, with light toast and caramel and high carbonation, and was served very fresh.
children.yearLabel: after the Civil War (c. 1865) until Prohibition

children.name: Pre-Prohibition Lager
children.description: A bitter, hoppy pale American adjunct lager, the German-immigrant "Classic American Pilsner", often with a robust corn flavor, more body and far more hops than modern American lager.
children.yearLabel: mid-1800s; most popular from the 1870s until 1919; homebrew revival 1990s

parents.note: Adaptation of continental pale lager by immigrant German brewers, using native six-row barley, corn or rice, and American hops; "Classic American Pilsner".

children.name: Burton Ale
children.description: The strong, sweetish, dark-amber to brown ale that made Burton-upon-Trent famous before IPA (Bass No. 1, Ind Coope). It is rich and fruity with a firm hop bitterness, and later survived as winter warmers. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.
children.yearLabel: late 1700s (Baltic trade), then domestic through the 1900s

children.name: World Traditional & Indigenous
children.description: Living folk beers outside the European brewing mainstream, made from rye bread or sorghum, often low in alcohol and sour.

children.name: Kvass
children.description: A traditional Slavic and Baltic low-alcohol fermented drink of rye bread or rye malt. It is sweet-tart, bready and sometimes flavored with mint or raisins, and is sold in bulk from street tankers and in PET bottles. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.

children.name: Sorghum Beer (Umqombothi / Opaque Beer)
children.description: A traditional Southern and Central African opaque, sour, porridge-like beer of malted sorghum and maize (umqombothi), drunk while still fermenting. Industrial versions sell in "shake shake" cartons, and clear sorghum lagers are a modern offshoot. No BJCP or BA ranges exist, so the ranges are approximate, taken from historical accounts and modern examples.

origin.country: Southern & Central Africa (South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Uganda)

hops: None (traditional); light hopping in sorghum lagers
children.yeast: Wild/mixed yeast and Lactobacillus (traditional); commercial ale or lager yeast

topSellers.name: Chibuku Shake Shake
topSellers.brewery: Delta Beverages and other AB InBev affiliates
